The famous ship that sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg is the RMS Titanic.

To understand blockchain technology, imagine a massive, shared notebook that is distributed among thousands of people instead of being kept in a single office. In a traditional system, like a bank's database, one central authority keeps the only copy of the ledger. If that central server is hacked or the person in charge makes a mistake, the records can be altered or lost.

In the blockchain analogy, every person in the network holds an identical copy of this notebook. When a new transaction occurs, it is written into a "page" (or block) of the notebook. Before this page is added to the notebook, everyone checks the math to ensure it is correct. Once the majority agrees it is valid, the page is sealed with a unique digital stamp (a cryptographic hash) and added to the chain.

Because every copy of the notebook is linked to the previous one, changing a single entry in the past would require changing every subsequent page in every single notebook across the entire network simultaneously. This is practically impossible, which is why the system is considered immutable and secure. It removes the need for a central trusted authority, as trust is placed in the consensus of the network and the mathematical verification of the data.
